# North Pacific Strategy Initiative — full machine-readable index

> An independent research imprint publishing reference-grade working papers on Pacific sovereignty, bilateral financial architecture, and the defensive options available to middle powers in a period of dollar-system stress. Edited in Victoria, British Columbia. Working-paper text is licensed CC-BY-4.0; the imprint and wordmark are not licensed.

This file is the full-content companion to https://npsi.ca/llms.txt. It carries
the complete abstract, key findings, and citation metadata for every document
the imprint has published. Content is current as of 29 July 2026.

How to cite: "Jesse James, *[Title]*, NPSI Working Paper No. [N] (North Pacific
Strategy Initiative, [Month Year]), https://npsi.ca/wp[N]/." Substitute
Technical Briefing / Briefing Note / Special Briefing and the matching URL for
the other series. Document IDs follow NPSI-WP-NNN (working papers), NPSI-TB-NNN
(technical briefings), NPSI-BN-NNN (briefing notes), NPSI-SB-NNN (special
briefings). Where a PDF exists it is the canonical release document; every
document also has a full HTML reading view at its canonical URL with Highwire
citation_* meta tags and Schema.org JSON-LD. Editor: Jesse James
(editor@npsi.ca). Numbering is the author's: WP6 and WP8 are unreleased, so the
archive carries intentional gaps at 6 and 8.

## Working Paper No. 11 — Rated AAA by the Issuer

- ID: NPSI-WP-011 · Technical Series · v1.0 · 28 July 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp11/ · PDF (18 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp11/working-paper.pdf
- Status: the current working paper. Supersedes WP10, which remains available unaltered with a correction notice.
- Keywords: open source AI, credit ratings, quality labels, base rates, forecasting, OSAID, EU AI Act, open weights, certification, capability thresholds

Abstract: There is no enforced definition of open source in artificial
intelligence. A standards body wrote one and cannot compel anyone to use it; a
regulator wrote a different one that binds in a single jurisdiction; a
procurement authority expressed a preference for the thing and never defined it
at all. In that vacuum, the company that builds a model is the party that
declares it open — the labeller is the labelled. The closest precedent is not
open-source software but the credit rating. The paper corrects its predecessor
(WP-10) in a published correction notice, establishes that the July 2026 policy
fight is not about whether to ban open-weight models but about who defines
"sufficiently capable," and applies documented base rates from four other
markets that ran unenforced quality labels to produce a forecast, with
probabilities, of how this one resolves.

Key findings: Four itemised corrections to WP10 are published at §1, including
the framing correction that Anthropic is the most restriction-friendly major
lab on open weights and has not called for a ban — both halves true. Both camps
in the July 2026 fight (the 24 July Nvidia-hosted multi-signatory letter and
Anthropic) reject a categorical ban in writing; the live leverage is in who
defines the capability threshold, which falls disproportionately on open
releases because guardrails cannot be reimposed after weights ship. The
base-rate table covers four label markets — organic (resolved by statute after
~12 years), Energy Star (certifier hardening after GAO-10-470), credit ratings
(statute after systemic failure), and "natural" (never resolved) — and the §5
forecast assigns probabilities with named falsifiers: label decays 45%,
certifier gets teeth 20%, capability capture 25%, certifier captured 10%.
Author's disclosure: drafted with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), whose
statements the paper examines.

## Working Paper No. 9 — The Counterparty Problem

- ID: NPSI-WP-009 · v1.0 · 27 July 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp9/ · PDF (12 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp9/working-paper.pdf
- Companions: WP1 (counterparty-diversification thesis), SB2 (the EXIM SCRI door)
- Keywords: export credit, EXIM, Memorandum of Understanding, treaty withdrawal, commitment reliability, counterparty risk, sovereign wealth funds, reauthorization, Congress, Public Investment Fund

Abstract: U.S. reliability is not one question but two, and conflating them
produces bad risk analysis. The United States has a real, documented and
recently accelerating record of formally exiting binding treaties — roughly
fifteen significant withdrawals or repudiations since 2001 — but no honest
failure-to-convert base rate can be computed for non-binding instruments like
MoUs, because no registry of U.S. MoUs exists. The paper assesses the
24 July 2026 PIF–EXIM $15 billion MoU against the sharpest available case
study: EXIM's 2015–2019 board-quorum lapse, which cut the bank's financing by
almost 85 percent, and a charter that expires again on 31 December 2026 with
reauthorization still in committee.

Key findings: Formal withdrawals cluster in 2017–2020 and 2025–2026. The
PIF–EXIM instrument is explicitly non-binding; EXIM's charter expires
31 December 2026, with the Senate's ten-year extension bill in committee and no
markup. During the 2015–2019 quorum lapse, financing declined roughly 85
percent, and each dollar of EXIM financing supports approximately $4.50 of
exports. The paper's balance is load-bearing: it concedes democratic policy
alternation, the honoured-commitment record (NATO Article 5, Bretton Woods, the
Japan and Korea treaties), and that other states have worse records. The
framing is counterparty-risk pricing, not anti-American critique.

## Working Paper No. 10 — Fair Use for We, IP Theft for Thee

- ID: NPSI-WP-010 · Technical Series · v1.0 · 26 July 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp10/ · PDF (17 pp., canonical): https://npsi.ca/wp10/working-paper.pdf
- Status: superseded by WP11 (corrections itemised at its §1); remains available unaltered with a correction notice attached.
- Keywords: open source AI, OSAID, open weights, model licences, Llama, EU AI Act, fair use, distillation, copyright litigation, procurement, Canada

Abstract: Between 16 and 24 July 2026 the United States government came closer
to restricting foreign open-weight AI models than at any point in the
technology's existence — and not one of the statements driving that policy
rests on an agreed definition of the thing being restricted. The paper reads
the licences: of eleven major model families surveyed, three satisfy the Open
Source Initiative's definition, and none of those three operates at frontier
scale. Llama 4's licence withholds rights from anyone domiciled in the European
Union, inside a product marketed as open source, in the one jurisdiction that
offers open-source models a regulatory exemption. And the characterisation now
driving policy — that training on another party's output is fair use when
American labs do it and theft when Chinese labs do it — is real at the level of
framing, weaker than advertised at the level of evidence, and applied to
conduct that three separate bodies of law treat three separate ways.

Key findings: OSAID v1.0 (October 2024) has been adopted as a binding criterion
by no regulator or procurement authority located in the survey; of eleven model
families, three meet the definition (OLMo 2, Pythia/GPT-NeoX, arguably BLOOM),
none at frontier scale. The paper's spine is a three-category legal separation:
taking model weights is theft, uncontested; training on scraped outputs is
contested and litigated; acquiring pirated corpora has been adjudicated against
the lab (the Bartz v. Anthropic settlement). Every claim is evidence-graded
VERIFIED / CORROBORATED / ATTRIBUTED / UNDETERMINED. Author's disclosure:
drafted with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), whose conduct §6 examines.
Read with WP11's correction notice.

## Working Paper No. 7 — Dazzle 2.0

- ID: NPSI-WP-007 · Counter-Autonomy Series (first paper) · v1.0 · 12 July 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp7/ · PDF (10 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp7/working-paper.pdf
- Companion: TB1 — The Verified Sky (the sensing substrate)
- Keywords: adversarial machine learning, dazzle camouflage, machine vision, drones, counter-autonomy, loitering munitions, sensor fusion, procurement, NATO, Canada

Abstract: Russian logistics trucks in Ukraine have worn high-contrast dazzle
paint since late May 2026, and the intent — degrading the machine vision on
strike drones — is accepted by serious analysts. But no controlled test shows
the tactic defeating any named detector. The durable finding is cost asymmetry:
a paint can iterates in an afternoon; a fielded detector re-learns only as fast
as its slowest update loop. The paper separates confirmed fact from inference
and hype, and draws the procurement lesson for NATO and Canada: vision-only
terminal guidance is brittle; sensor fusion, human authorization, and
edge-retrainable models are the robust answers.

Key findings: Every load-bearing claim is tagged Confirmed / Plausible /
Speculation / Hype in the §2 evidence table. The most plausible mechanism is
out-of-distribution confusion, not an engineered adversarial attack; three gaps
(optimization, physical robustness, transferability) separate crude stripes
from the academically proven ceiling (Eykholt et al. CVPR 2018; adversarial
patches; CAMOU-class vehicle textures). The durable finding is cost asymmetry,
anchored to the CENTCOM aircraft-tire case where the retraining loop ran up to
six months. Five procurement recommendations: multi-sensor seekers,
human-on-the-loop authorization, edge-retrainable models with organic
labeling, adversarial and out-of-distribution inputs in acceptance testing, and
no single-vendor black-box automatic target recognition.

## Working Paper No. 5 — Sovereign Compute North

- ID: NPSI-WP-005 · v1.0 · 27 May 2026 · Co-issued with Fit For Gov
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp5/ · PDF (19 pp., canonical): https://npsi.ca/wp5/working-paper.pdf
- Companion: SB1 — Zero Secrets (the exposure audit)
- Keywords: data sovereignty, sovereign cloud, Canada, Korea, HBM, hydroelectricity, data centres, CLOUD Act, sovereign compute, municipal infrastructure

Abstract: Canada has the cheapest low-carbon firm electricity in the G7. Korea
controls the global memory chokepoint on which every modern AI accelerator
depends. The United States has stated, under oath through Microsoft France in
June 2025, that it cannot guarantee allied citizens' data against US
extraterritorial reach. The trade is obvious: Canadian electrons, Korean
memory, Canadian law, Korean and allied capital — combined into a
government-owned compute fabric that reaches from the Hydro-Québec switchyard
to the municipal town hall.

Key findings: An energy-for-memory swap signed under Canadian law — a
government-owned, allies-financed, Canadian-law-bound compute fabric anchored
on surplus Canadian power and Korea-led sovereign capital, extended to the
municipal layer. The paper specifies the control-based sovereignty test
(jurisdictional, operational, cryptographic, audit), the five Canadian Digital
Sovereignty Standard clauses, the provincial power inventory, and the capital
stack. Sits inside the three-rail Pacific architecture with WP1 (financial
rail) and WP2 (energy/compute rail).

## Working Paper No. 4 — The Addition Paradox

- ID: NPSI-WP-004 · v1.0 · 15 May 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp4/ · PDF: https://npsi.ca/wp4/working-paper.pdf
- Keywords: Canada, energy transition, oil sands, hydroelectricity, uranium, critical minerals, clean-energy concentration, Pacific export capacity

Abstract: Why the energy transition did not happen, why that is acceptable, and
why Canada is uniquely positioned to win the forty years that follow. A record
year for clean-energy deployment was also a record year for fossil combustion:
the global system did not transition, it expanded.

Key findings: 2024 saw a record 858 TWh of new clean electricity and record
fossil combustion; global electricity demand grew 1,172 TWh, so fossil supplied
the remaining 314 TWh; coal remains the largest single source into the
mid-2030s. Chokepoint risk migrated from molecules to minerals: clean-tech
refining and assembly concentrate in a single nation (polysilicon ≈95%, lithium
cells ≈80%, NdFeB magnets ≈90%) — framed as concentration risk, not as an
argument against clean energy. Canada holds four assets on one hand: the
third-largest oil reserves with the lowest-carbon barrel trajectory, the
largest per-capita clean electricity in the industrial democracies, the
second-largest high-grade uranium reserves (Athabasca Basin), and the only G7
position with simultaneous Pacific and Atlantic deepwater export capacity.
Strategic preface to the three-rail architecture (WP1, WP2, WP3).

## Working Paper No. 3 — A Canada–Korea Pacific Defence-Industrial Corridor

- ID: NPSI-WP-003 · v1.0.1 · May 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp3/ · PDF (30 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp3/working-paper.pdf
- Keywords: Canada, Korea, CPSP, submarines, KSS-III, Hanwha, defence-industrial, bilateral defence cooperation, CKFTA, SDCP

Abstract: A bilateral defence-industrial architecture pairing the Canadian
Patrol Submarine Project with the Hanwha–Algoma Steel and Hanwha–APMA
industrial-offset structures, anchored to the CKFTA institutional foundation,
the October 2025 SDCP, and the 25 February 2026 Foreign and Defence (2+2)
Ministerial Joint Statement.

Key findings: The Canadian Patrol Submarine Project (up to 12 boats by 2035;
Hanwha Ocean and TKMS confirmed as the two qualified suppliers, 19 August 2025)
read against Korea's offset posture: the binding Hanwha–Algoma MOU
(26 January 2026) and the conditional Hanwha–APMA MOU (29 April 2026), with the
30 October 2025 Carney–Lee Security and Defence Cooperation Partnership as the
institutional anchor. Completes the three-rail Pacific architecture as the
defence-industrial rail alongside WP1 (financial) and WP2 (energy/compute).

## Working Paper No. 2 — A Canada–United States Energy and Compute Compact

- ID: NPSI-WP-002 · v1.0 · May 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp2/ · PDF (45 pp.): https://npsi.ca/wp2/working-paper.pdf
- Keywords: Canada, United States, CUSMA, AI compute, hydroelectricity, ultra-high-voltage transmission, bilateral compact

Abstract: A treaty-grade bilateral architecture pairing Canadian dispatchable
generation with the U.S. grid through ultra-high-voltage transmission, siting
AI training workloads on Canadian hydro-electric capacity, and preserving
inference workloads at the U.S. urban edge. Structurally complementary to
Working Paper No. 1; financed through the same supranational vehicle.

Key findings: The U.S. faces a structural capacity gap (~44 GW required by 2028
against ~25 GW deliverable); combined dispatchable Canadian hydro is
approximately 56,000 MW across Hydro-Québec, BC Hydro, and Manitoba Hydro. AI
workloads bifurcate — training is latency-agnostic and can sit on Canadian
hydro, inference stays at the U.S. urban edge — and roughly 80 percent of AI
critical-IT load is inference by 2030. Three corridor candidates
(Saguenay/Côte-Nord, Peace River/Bennett, Northern Manitoba), an Indigenous
Series II tranche of 10–15 percent of compact capex, and survival independent
of CUSMA renewal.

## Working Paper No. 1 — The Bilateral Foundation

- ID: NPSI-WP-001 · v1.0 · May 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/wp1/ · PDF: https://npsi.ca/wp1/working-paper.pdf
- Keywords: Canada, Korea, sovereign bonds, CKPIF, Pacific architecture, bilateral finance, middle-power policy

Abstract: A thirty-year Canada–Korea co-issued sovereign infrastructure bond —
assembled from off-the-shelf instruments, priced as a spread over US
Treasuries, with Indigenous co-ownership embedded at issuance — as the
architecture of middle-power independence.

Key findings: Proposes the Canada–Korea Pacific Infrastructure Facility
(CKPIF): a treaty-based supranational issuer with 50/50 ownership, Luxembourg
seat, English law, and LCIA arbitration; indicative programme size US$25–40
billion over 5–7 years, priced indicatively +50–80 bp over 30-year US
Treasuries; several (not joint) sovereign guarantees. An Indigenous Series I
tranche of 10–15 percent of programme with +25 bp ratchet protection; KPI
architecture on ICMA Sustainability-Linked Bond Principles; a tokenised pilot
tranche of US$200–500 million on Project Agorá-class infrastructure. The
institutional foundation is the Bank of Canada–Bank of Korea standing swap
line, signed November 2017, with no expiry and no preset limit.

## Technical Briefing No. 1 — The Verified Sky

- ID: NPSI-TB-001 · v1.0 · 11 June 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/tb1/ · PDF: https://npsi.ca/tb1/technical-briefing.pdf
- Keywords: airspace awareness, computer vision, sensor fusion, counter-UAS, Remote ID, verification architecture, edge AI, Canada, Radiocommunication Act, PIPEDA

Abstract: A survey of the 2025–2026 state of the art in computer vision and
sensing for monitoring a defined volume of airspace; the verification
architecture that converts a probabilistic detection into a near-certain
identification; realistic detection-to-action latency; the statutory line
between lawful and criminal automated response for a private Canadian operator;
and a deliberately conservative capability forecast at one, two-and-a-half, and
five years.

Key findings: The signature element is the verification ledger — seven
conditions (class, size, altitude, kinematics, window, geofence, persistence)
that must all pass before any action fires, with two-sensor corroboration as
the standing industry rule. Benchmark honesty: realistic small-and-distant
detection performance runs at roughly half of headline benchmark performance.
The Canadian legal line: detection, tracking, evidence, and notification are
lawful for civil operators; jamming, spoofing, takeover, and physical downing
are not. Explicitly a technical and regulatory survey, not legal advice.

## Briefing Note No. 1 — The Voter File

- ID: NPSI-BN-001 · v1.0 · 11 June 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/bn1/ · PDF: https://npsi.ca/bn1/briefing-note.pdf
- Keywords: voter files, political parties, privacy law, Canada Elections Act, Bill C-4, PIPEDA, data-driven campaigning, microtargeting

Abstract: Every major Canadian federal political party maintains a database
with a record on substantially every voter, assembled in five layers: the
Elections Canada list of electors, canvassing observations, appended public
records, appended commercial data, and modelled behavioural scores. No layer
requires consent; no layer grants a right of access. In March 2026, Part 4 of
Bill C-4 excluded federal parties from provincial and territorial privacy law,
retroactive to 2000.

Key findings: The five-layer file documented end to end, with the legal
chronology: PIPEDA never applied; Bill C-76 (2018) required only a published
privacy policy; BC OIPC Order P22-02 (2022) and the 2024 BC Supreme Court
judicial review found BC PIPA could apply; Bill C-4 Part 4 (royal assent
March 2026) closed that path retroactive to 2000, with the Senate's three-year
sunset amendment rejected. Explicitly non-partisan; the illustrative voter
record is fictional and labelled as such.

## Special Briefing No. 3 — The Ledger With One Entry

- ID: NPSI-SB-003 · v1.0 · issued 26 July 2026 (reporting cut-off 22 July 2026); integrated 29 July 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb3/ · PDF (39 pp., canonical): https://npsi.ca/sb3/special-briefing.pdf
- Companions: WP9 (counterparty reliability), WP1 (diversification thesis), SB1 (jurisdictional exposure)
- Keywords: Venezuela, oil revenue, asset custody, sanctions, escrow, accountability, TRIA, Crystallex, oil-for-food, counterparty risk

Abstract: Since United States forces captured Nicolás Maduro on 3 January 2026,
the American government has controlled the sale of Venezuelan crude oil and the
disposition of its proceeds. The Financial Times estimates those sales have
raised more than US$13 billion; Venezuela's own transparency portal records a
single receipt of $300 million, and no audit has been published. The briefing
verifies the factual record, prices the gap, explains the legal architecture
that produced the offshore structure — two traps in American law that would
have destroyed the funds on arrival — and benchmarks the arrangement against
the three comparable oil-custody regimes of the past quarter-century. It
reaches an uncomfortable conclusion: the Venezuela mechanism is the least
accountable of the four, and the most accountable of them still lost
$8.8 billion.

Key findings: The offshore structure is not evidence of intent to steal — TRIA
§201 attachment and the Crystallex alter-ego doctrine (932 F.3d 126) would
have destroyed the funds on arrival in a U.S. account; the structure built to
defeat Venezuela's creditors also defeats the United States Congress. Four
custody regimes benchmarked (Iraq OFF/DFI, Libya, Iran/Qatar 2023, Venezuela):
Venezuela is the least accountable; Iraq, the most accountable, still lost
$8.8 billion (SIGIR). The intervention redirected rather than interrupted the
oil (1.23m b/d April 2026, highest since 2018); Shandong's independent
refiners were the largest single loser — the Pacific consequence. Every
material claim confidence-rated; both governments flagged as interested
parties; four named unclassified documents would settle the accounting.

## Special Briefing No. 2 — The Three Doors

- ID: NPSI-SB-002 · v1.0 · 2 July 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb2/ · PDF (canonical): https://npsi.ca/sb2/special-briefing.pdf
- Keywords: critical minerals, Defense Production Act, domestic source, Canada, mining finance, DPA Title III, Energy Act 18743, EXIM, supply chain

Abstract: Under U.S. defense law, Canada has been a domestic source since 1992
(50 U.S.C. §4552). Canadian companies qualify for American defense-industrial
grants, loans, and loan guarantees on the same footing as a firm in Ohio. This
briefing maps the three doors — Defense Production Act Title III, Energy Act of
2020 §18743, and the Export-Import Bank's Supply Chain Resiliency Initiative —
and the navigation moat that stalls applicants.

Key findings: A ten-panel briefing built around the 1992 domestic-source
provision and the three federal funding doors it opens for Canadian critical-
minerals producers, with the navigation moat — not eligibility — identified as
the binding constraint.

## Special Briefing No. 1 — Zero Secrets

- ID: NPSI-SB-001 · v1.0 · 11 June 2026
- Canonical: https://npsi.ca/sb1/ · PDF: https://npsi.ca/sb1/special-briefing.pdf
- Companion: WP5 — Sovereign Compute North (the constructive proposal)
- Keywords: data sovereignty, CLOUD Act, FISA 702, sovereign AI, sovereign compute, cloud jurisdiction, Investment Canada Act, Canada

Abstract: Canada effectively holds no data secrets from the United States — not
by choice, but by architecture. The overwhelming majority of Canadian
government, corporate, and citizen data sits on infrastructure owned by three
American corporations, and under the US CLOUD Act and FISA Section 702,
American jurisdiction follows corporate ownership, not server location. This
briefing audits the exposure, the federal response, and the demonstrated
capability class, and recommends a three-stage sovereign-infrastructure
response.

Key findings: Data residency is not data sovereignty — under the CLOUD Act
(18 U.S.C. §2713) and FISA 702, US jurisdiction follows corporate ownership,
not server location, and no Canada–US CLOUD Act bilateral exists. Anchor
evidence includes Microsoft France's sworn testimony before the French Senate
(10 June 2025). Recommends a control-based definition of sovereign cloud
(jurisdictional, operational, cryptographic, audit), migration of classified
and Protected B workloads, and Canadian-owned-and-operated awards. The caveats
section states the strongest counter-cases (cost, Five Eyes, free-riding)
fairly.

- Commentary: https://npsi.ca/commentary/ — named commentary index, per paper.
